ER Tip 1: When you feel stuck, pick one small step you feel you can do and start with that.
ER Tip 2: Try the Pomodoro method: take a 5 minute break after every 30 minutes of work for your mind to rejuvenate.
ER Tip 3: Take a deep breath, and think about how nice it will feel when the task you are working on is finally complete.
ER Tip 4: Give yourself something to look forward to after you finish studying, such as seeing a movie or getting a meal with friends.
ER Tip 5: Before you begin studying, take a moment to jot down how you're feeling, and what goals you can meet based on how you're feeling.
ER Tip 6: When you lack motivation, move to a new, comfortable study/work spot such as a library or coffee shop.
ER Tip 7: If an assignment feels scary, choose a certain time of day when you tend to feel most motivated to try and complete it.
ER Tip 8: When you feel overwhelmed about a certain task, remind yourself of all that you have already done and take pride in what you have accomplished, even if it was a small step.
ER Tip 9: If you feel overwhelmed by the work you have to do, see if you can reward yourself by crossing off small items on your to-do list
ER Tip 10: Identify the context of your situation by asking yourself: “What is the challenge that I’m facing?” Making this explicit can help you identify your goals and the steps needed to achieve them.
ER Tip 11: If you have a big task, try to break it down into at least three smaller steps.
ER Tip 12: When facing a difficult situation, try to find a way of handling it that feels right to you, regardless of how things might turn out.
ER Tip 13: If it feels overwhelming to prepare for your future career, remind yourself that you don't have to have it all figured out right now. You can only control what you're doing in the present moment.
ER Tip 14: If you are feeling stuck or overwhelmed, ask someone close to you if you can talk to them about how you are feeling and see if they may have advice to offer
ER Tip 15: If you feel it's time for a break from work, try to carve out some time during the week for you to do just that!
ER Tip 16: This assignment won't last forever. This time next week, it will probably be done.
ER Tip 17: Remember that "perfect" can be the enemy of "good".
ER Tip 18: Sometimes, it is better to get something done than have it completed perfectly.
ER Tip 19: If an assignment seems stressful, set a timer for ten minutes and see how much you can get done.
ER Tip 20: Try "body doubling" - some people get more work done when there's another person in the room.

ER Tip 1: Find an activity that can help you feel connected to someone you care about and who cares about you.
ER Tip 2: Strengthen the bond you have with a loved one by finding an interest you both share and talking about it.
ER Tip 3: Think of one thing about a loved one that you are thankful for, and how that has positively affected you.
ER Tip 4: It's okay if you need a break from your loved ones. Give yourself the space you need to recharge.
ER Tip 5: Use "I" statements (I feel ___ because ___) when you are communicating your emotions to a loved one.
ER Tip 6: Take space from loved ones if you feel overwhelmed.
ER Tip 7: If you feel homesick, schedule calls with loved ones to keep in touch.
ER Tip 8: When a conversation at home starts to feel tense, pause and take a few slow breaths before responding.
ER Tip 9: If you feel unsupported by your family at home, see if you can reach out to any friends who would be able to provide the support you feel you need.
ER Tip 10: When you feel a negative emotion toward a loved one, ask yourself if a friend or family member would feel the same way in your situation.
ER Tip 11: In difficult interactions, focus on what you can control and define your goals in terms of how your approach to the situation. Remember that you cannot control how other people feel and act.
ER Tip 12: Create a small routine with a family member, like a weekly meal or walk, that gives you something steady to look forward to.
ER Tip 13: It helps to remember that everyone has a different perspective. If you're having a hard time understanding why a loved one is acting a certain way, try considering the situation from their perspective.
ER Tip 14: When facing a difficult situation, try to find a way of handling it that feels right to you, regardless of how things might turn out.
ER Tip 15: If a disagreement at home is escalating, agree on a signal or phrase with a loved one that means "let's take a break and come back to this later."
ER Tip 16: Write down what you appreciate about your home environment, even during a hard week, to help balance out frustration.
ER Tip 17: Take time to identify if you want to connect with family members in the current moment. Honor this desire with your actions.
ER Tip 19: When you feel triggered by a family member's tone or comment, pause to ask yourself whether it's really about you before reacting.
ER Tip 20: If tension is building during a family activity, it's okay to step into another room for a few minutes before rejoining.

ER Tip 1: Before looking up the same question about your health online again, ask yourself if you are really seeking new infomration or just re-checking something. Reduce time spent re-checking.
ER Tip 2: Getting enough sleep can make a huge difference in how you feel both physically and mentally. Check in with your sleep schedule and see if there are ways you can increase sleep.
ER Tip 3: You might be feeling some pain in your body right now. Remind yourself that pain ebbs and flows and the pain likely won't stay this intense forever.
ER Tip 4: Think of times in your past when you were worried about an aspect of your physical health that ended up being perfectly normal.
ER Tip 5: If you notice that your heart is racing or you’re having trouble breathing, ask yourself if there might be a perfectly harmless explanation for why your body is reacting that way (e.g. did you just walk up a flight of stairs?)
ER Tip 6: If you notice that you’re not feeling well, remember that there are a variety of low-stakes reasons why you might be feeling that way (e.g., you may be tired, you may have eaten something bad, etc.)
ER Tip 7: Accept the emotions that you're having rather than judging yourself for having them.
ER Tip 8: When you're feeling overwhelmed, take a moment to notice three things in your environment that stick out to you (e.g., is the person sitting next to you wearing cool shoes?)
ER Tip 9: Take a moment to appreciate your body for supporting you through life.
ER Tip 10: When you experience an uncomfortable bodily sensation (e.g., racing heart or sweaty palms), simply sit with that sensation for a moment before you react to it. These sensations often pass quickly without any intervention.
ER Tip 11: Is there a time over the next day or two when you think you'll feel anxious? Consider setting an alarm to remind yourself to practice flexible thinking in that moment.
ER Tip 12: All emotions serve a purpose. They tell us about what's going on in our lives and help motivate us. Even the negative feelings, like fear and anxiety, help us navigate the world around us.
ER Tip 13: Every body is different. Take a moment to appreciate all that your body does to keep you alive.
ER Tip 14: Set a time/date when you will make a decision about whether you need to see a doctor (e.g., if I still feel sick 3 days from now, I will schedule an appointment)
ER Tip 15: If you are experiencing physical discomfort, try to notice and name what you are experiencing. Remind yourself that discomfort usually passes or gets less intense over time.
ER Tip 16: All feelings pass. When it feels like a negative feeling (like sadness or fear) will never end, gently remind yourself that this feeling will eventually pass.
ER Tip 17: Remember that researching your health symptoms on the internet can often lead to an anxiety spiral. Try asking a close friend if you can confide in them about the way you are feeling.
ER Tip 18: If you've been tired recently, try putting away your phone half an hour before bedtime.
ER Tip 19: Ask yourself if your social needs are being met. (Do you want to be around others right now? Do you want to be alone?) Allow yourself to honor these needs by letting people around you know how you are feeling and what you need.
ER Tip 20: Try to put a specific label on your feelings (are you sad, angry, disgusted, nervous, terrfiied, etc.?) - feelings are easier to manage when we can describe them fully.

ER Tip 1: Give yourself a challenge to speak to someone new.
ER Tip 2: Renewing old friendships can be as rewarding as starting new ones.
ER Tip 3: Try to imagine yourself as an outsider watching your conversation. Ask yourself if they would think about how you're doing in the same way you are.
ER Tip 4: Rather than only focusing on negative moments you've spent with friends, also think about positive ones. Remind yourself of all the times when you've smiled and laughed together.
ER Tip 5: When you feel like comparing yourself to others in your life, try to give yourself a compliment instead.
ER Tip 6: Think about something positive that happened when you interacted with someone today and savor how you felt during that experience
ER Tip 7: Allow yourself to take a step back from friendships or relationships that you feel are negatively affecting you.
ER Tip 8: If you are struggling to start a conversation with someone, think of a compliment or kind word to share with them.
ER Tip 9: If you feel overwhelmed by interacting with new people, take time for yourself to recharge your social battery.
ER Tip 10: Think of a time in the past when a one-on-one social event went well.
ER Tip 11: If you notice yourself replaying an interaction from earlier in the day over and over again, it can be helpful to distract yourself with an enjoyable or soothing activity, like watching TV or playing with a pet.
ER Tip 12: Plan on stepping out of your comfort zone, even in a small way. Sometimes it helps to ask someone else - like a friend or loved one - to help hold you accountable.
ER Tip 13: When angry or upset about any situation, let that emotion come and go. Rather than trying to push it away, allow yourself to acknowledge and deeply feel your emotions safely.
ER Tip 14: Remind yourself that most social moments that you fixate on are quickly forgotten by others.
ER Tip 15: If you have been feeling upset in a friendship, try to clearly express what you need or how you feel to your friend, while being open to their perspective.
ER Tip 16: Mind reading can be tempting when disagreeing with a friend. Instead of assuming you know what your friend is thinking, try asking questions about their perspective.
ER Tip 17: If you find yourself ruminating about an upcoming social event, remember that you can't predict the future.
ER Tip 18: Before a social event that feels overwhelming, plan a small way to step outside or take a breather if you need one.
ER Tip 19: If a conversation leaves you feeling anxious, remind yourself that you can't know for sure what someone else is thinking, so try not to fill in the blanks with worst-case guesses.
ER Tip 20: Practice naming your emotion in the moment (like "I feel embarrassed" or "I feel left out") — putting a word to the feeling can make it easier to manage.

ER Tip 1: If you find yourself feeling angry during a conversation with your partner, try expressing your thoughts and feelings calmly rather than yelling or making accusations.
ER Tip 2: Try to imagine something from your partner's point of view.
ER Tip 3: If you get into a disagreement with a partner, consider acknowledging your differences and how they may affect the way you react to situations.
ER Tip 4: Use "I" statements (I feel ___ because ___) when you are communicating your emotions to a partner. And, try not to use "you" statements (You are being ___).
ER Tip 5: Mind reading can be tempting when disagreeing with a partner. Instead of assuming you know what your partner is thinking, try asking questions about their perspective.
ER Tip 6: Sometimes it's helpful to take a few minutes to cool off if you're upset with your partner. Try taking a break from arguing for 5 minutes, and then come back together to try to talk about the issue again.
ER Tip 7: If you feel jealous or insecure, try to name the specific worry behind the feeling before reacting or saying something you don't mean.
ER Tip 8: If a text goes unanswered for a while, remind yourself there are lots of harmless reasons for a delay before assuming the worst.
ER Tip 9: Give yourself permission to take space from a partner if you're feeling overwhelmed, rather than reacting right away.
ER Tip 10: Before comparing your relationship to others you see online, remember that most people only post their highlights.
ER Tip 11: If a disagreement starts to feel heated, agree with your partner on a way to pause and revisit the conversation once you've both calmed down.
ER Tip 12: Remind yourself that a partner's mood or bad day isn't always about you.
ER Tip 13: If you're frustrated with your partner, ask yourself if you have communicated your feelings or if you're expecting them to read your mind. Sometimes we don't notice when we expect our loved ones to know what we're thinking.
ER Tip 14: If your romantic partner is upset, try asking them what they might need from you in that moment.
ER Tip 15: Communicate to your partner about how you are feeling and what you think you might need from them in order to feel better.
ER Tip 16: Celebrate small, positive moments in the relationship instead of only focusing on what feels uncertain.
ER Tip 17: Spend time with people you care about who are outside of your relationship (friends, family, etc.).
ER Tip 18: If you have been feeling upset in your relationship, try to clearly express what you need or how you feel to your partner, while being open to their perspective.
ER Tip 19: If you're feeling anxious about the relationship's pace, remind yourself that people move at different speeds, and that's okay.
ER Tip 20: Talk to a trusted friend or family member about how you're feeling instead of keeping worries bottled up.

ER Tip 1: If a post doesn't get the likes or comments you expected, remind yourself that this doesn't reflect how much people actually care about you.
ER Tip 2: Before comparing your life to what you see online, remember that most people only post their highlights, not their struggles.
ER Tip 3: If you feel a wave of comparison scrolling through your feed, try taking a short break from the app before reacting.
ER Tip 4: Remind yourself that not seeing a reply right away doesn't mean someone is upset with you — they might just be busy.
ER Tip 5: If a post or comment upsets you, pause before responding and give yourself time to figure out how you actually want to react.
ER Tip 6: Set a specific time to check social media instead of scrolling anytime you feel anxious or bored.
ER Tip 7: If you notice yourself feeling worse after using an app, it's okay to mute, unfollow, or take a break from accounts that bring up hard feelings.
ER Tip 8: Remind yourself that a single photo or post is only a small snapshot, not the full picture of someone's life.
ER Tip 9: Before posting something, ask yourself how you'll feel about it later, not just in the moment.
ER Tip 10: If you're waiting anxiously for a like, comment, or reply, try shifting your attention to an activity you enjoy instead of refreshing the app.
ER Tip 11: If you see a friend hanging out with others without you, remind yourself there are many reasons you might not have been included that have nothing to do with you.
ER Tip 12: Notice if you're using social media to avoid a feeling instead of dealing with it, and try naming that feeling instead.
ER Tip 13: If a stranger's comment upsets you, remember their opinion doesn't define your worth.
ER Tip 14: Before reacting to a post that seems aimed at you, consider that it might not be about you at all.
ER Tip 15: Give yourself permission to log off during moments that matter in real life, even if it means missing something online.
ER Tip 16: If comparing follower counts or likes starts to feel stressful, remind yourself that these numbers don't measure your value as a person.
ER Tip 17: Follow accounts that make you feel good and consider muting ones that consistently leave you feeling anxious or inadequate.
ER Tip 18: If you're tempted to check on an ex's or a crush's profile, pause and ask yourself whether it will help or hurt how you feel afterward.
ER Tip 19: Remember that photos and videos are often edited or carefully chosen, so they rarely show the full story.
ER Tip 20: If you feel triggered by a viral trend or debate online, ground yourself by focusing on something happening right in front of you.

ER Tip 1: If you make a mistake during a game, take a deep breath and remind yourself that one play doesn't define your overall performance.
ER Tip 2: Before a big game or meet, try a few slow breaths to help calm pre-competition nerves.
ER Tip 3: If you're benched or pulled from a play, remind yourself it doesn't always mean you did something wrong.
ER Tip 4: Compare your progress to your own past performance instead of constantly measuring yourself against teammates.
ER Tip 5: If a coach's feedback stings in the moment, try to hear it as information to improve rather than a judgment of your worth.
ER Tip 6: Give yourself credit for effort and improvement, not just for winning or a perfect performance.
ER Tip 7: If you're nervous before competing, try a short routine — like stretching or listening to music — that helps you feel more grounded.
ER Tip 8: Remind yourself that feeling nervous before a game is normal and doesn't mean something is wrong.
ER Tip 9: After a tough loss, allow yourself to feel disappointed for a bit before shifting your focus to what you can learn from it.
ER Tip 10: If you're comparing your body or fitness level to teammates, remember that strength and endurance develop differently for everyone.
ER Tip 11: Use positive self-talk, like reminding yourself "I've prepared for this," when nerves start to build.
ER Tip 12: If frustration builds during a tough practice, take a short pause to reset before continuing.
ER Tip 13: Celebrate small wins, like a personal best or a skill you've improved, not just overall results.
ER Tip 14: If you're anxious about being cut or losing a starting spot, remind yourself that your value isn't only based on playing time.
ER Tip 15: Talk to a teammate, coach, or family member if pressure to perform starts to feel like too much.
ER Tip 16: Remind yourself that recovery and rest are part of getting stronger, not a sign of falling behind.
ER Tip 17: If you're struggling to learn a new skill or play, remind yourself that mastering something new usually takes practice and patience.
ER Tip 18: Before comparing your season or stats to others, remember that everyone's path and timeline in a sport looks different.
ER Tip 19: If nerves show up physically, like a racing heart or shaky hands, remind yourself this is just your body getting ready to perform.
ER Tip 20: After a game, take a moment to reflect on one thing that went well, even if the overall result wasn't what you hoped for.

ER Tip 1: Give yourself something to look forward to after you finish working, such as seeing a movie or getting a meal with friends.
ER Tip 2: Think about one fun thing you'll plan to buy with your next paycheck.
ER Tip 3: When you feel overwhelmed about a certain task, remind yourself of all that you have already done and take pride in what you have accomplished, even if it was a small step.
ER Tip 4: If you make a mistake at work, remind yourself that new employees are expected to learn as they go.
ER Tip 5: Before a shift that feels overwhelming, take a few slow breaths to help settle your nerves.
ER Tip 6: If a customer or coworker is short with you, remind yourself their mood is probably about their own day, not about you.
ER Tip 7: Give yourself credit for showing up and trying, even on days when the job feels hard.
ER Tip 8: If you're nervous before a job interview, remind yourself that feeling nervous doesn't mean you're unprepared.
ER Tip 9: Compare your progress at a new job to where you started, not to coworkers who've been there longer.
ER Tip 10: If your manager gives you corrective feedback, try to hear it as guidance for improving, not as a sign you're failing.
ER Tip 11: Take a short break, if you're able to, when you start to feel overwhelmed during a busy shift.
ER Tip 12: Remind yourself that asking a question when you're unsure is a normal part of learning a new job.
ER Tip 13: If you're anxious about your schedule or hours, talk to your manager directly instead of assuming the worst.
ER Tip 14: Celebrate small milestones, like finishing your first week or learning a new task, rather than focusing only on what you haven't mastered yet.
ER Tip 15: If comparing your job or paycheck to a friend's makes you feel behind, remind yourself that everyone's path looks different.
ER Tip 16: Use "I" statements (I feel ___ because ___) if you need to talk to a coworker or manager about something bothering you.
ER Tip 17: Remind yourself that one difficult shift doesn't reflect your overall ability to do the job.
ER Tip 18: If you're worried about being judged for your appearance or experience level, remember most people are focused on their own tasks.
ER Tip 19: Give yourself a moment to reset with a few deep breaths before responding to a frustrating situation at work.
ER Tip 20: Remind yourself that learning new equipment, systems, or routines takes time, even for people who look confident.

ER Tip 1: If news about climate change feels overwhelming, give yourself permission to take a break from the coverage for a while.
ER Tip 2: Focus your energy on one small action you can take, rather than trying to solve every part of the problem at once.
ER Tip 3: Remind yourself that solutions to climate change are still developing, even though the problem feels big and complex.
ER Tip 4: If you feel numb or exhausted by climate news instead of upset, remember that rest can protect your ability to care, not take it away.
ER Tip 5: Talk with friends or family about how you're feeling instead of carrying climate worries alone.
ER Tip 6: Remind yourself that meaningful change often happens in steps, not all at once.
ER Tip 7: If you feel guilty for not "doing enough," remember there are many different ways to show you care, and no single right way.
ER Tip 8: Balance time spent learning about climate issues with time spent on things that bring you joy or calm.
ER Tip 9: Remind yourself that your worth and effort aren't measured only by how much activism you do.
ER Tip 10: If you're overwhelmed imagining worst-case futures, try bringing your focus back to what's true and manageable right now.
ER Tip 11: Recognize that feeling upset about climate change is a sign you care, not a problem to fix about yourself.
ER Tip 12: If you're deciding whether to get involved in a climate group or cause, remember that commitment can look different for different people.
ER Tip 13: Remind yourself that systems and institutions do exist to help people adapt, even if they're imperfect.
ER Tip 14: Channel anxious energy into a concrete action, like learning something new or joining a project, rather than letting it sit unused.
ER Tip 15: If you feel like your individual actions don't matter, remember that change often starts before its effects are obvious.
ER Tip 16: Give yourself credit for caring about the future, even on days when it feels hard to stay hopeful.
ER Tip 17: Limit doom-scrolling climate content right before bed, since it can make it harder to wind down.
ER Tip 18: Remind yourself that uncertainty about the future is uncomfortable, but it doesn't mean the worst outcome is guaranteed.
ER Tip 19: If you feel isolated in your worry, look for others — friends, classmates, or online communities — who care about the same issues.
ER Tip 20: Remind yourself that you're allowed to hold both concern for the planet and hope for the future at the same time.

ER Tip 1: Remind yourself that milestones like driving, dating, or getting a job happen on different timelines for everyone, and there's no universal "right" schedule.
ER Tip 2: If a sibling or friend reaches a milestone before you, try to separate their timeline from what it means about your own path.
ER Tip 3: Celebrate the small steps toward a milestone, not just the moment it's officially reached.
ER Tip 4: If comparing yourself to peers who seem "ahead," remind yourself that growth and independence happen in stages
ER Tip 5: Give yourself patience when learning something new, like driving or budgeting, since most skills take practice before they feel natural.
ER Tip 6: Remind yourself that struggling with or delaying a milestone now doesn't mean you'll always be behind.
ER Tip 7: If you feel embarrassed about not having reached a milestone yet, remember that plenty of your peers are quietly feeling the same way.
ER Tip 8: Talk to a trusted adult or friend about milestone-related pressure instead of carrying the worry alone.
ER Tip 9: Remind yourself that physical changes, like growth spurts or puberty, happen on their own individual timeline.
ER Tip 10: If you feel anxious before a big first, like a job interview or driving test, remind yourself that nerves are a normal part of trying something new.
ER Tip 11: Focus on your own growth and progress rather than constantly measuring it against your friends' or siblings' milestones.
ER Tip 12: Remind yourself that failing at a milestone attempt, like a driving test, doesn't mean you won't succeed eventually.
ER Tip 13: If a milestone doesn't go the way you pictured, allow yourself to feel disappointed before shifting focus to what's next.
ER Tip 14: Remember that social media often only shows people's milestone highlights, not the setbacks along the way.
ER Tip 15: Give yourself credit for milestones that matter to you personally, even if they aren't highly visible to others.
ER Tip 16: Remind yourself that needing help from a parent or guardian a little longer doesn't mean you're less capable.
ER Tip 17: If you feel rushed to reach a milestone before you're ready, remember it's okay to move at your own pace.
ER Tip 18: Reflect on how far you've already come, rather than only focusing on what you haven't accomplished yet.
ER Tip 19: Remind yourself that a missed opportunity, like a school dance or trip, doesn't erase the other good memories you're building.
ER Tip 20: If you're nervous about a big change, like graduating or moving out, remind yourself that uncertainty is a normal part of growing up.
